claim: Sigma 1 receptor (S1R) is a 223-amino-acid-long transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein.
source: Sigma 1 receptor (S1R) is a 223-amino-acid-long transmembrane endoplasmic reticulum (ER) protein.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge about S1R structure.

claim: S1R modulates activity of multiple effector proteins.
source: S1R modulates activity of multiple effector proteins and is a well-established drug target.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: S1R is a well-established drug target.
source: S1R modulates activity of multiple effector proteins and is a well-established drug target.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Cholesterol directly affects S1R clustering.
source: By performing experiments in reduced reconstitution systems, we demonstrate direct effects of cholesterol on S1R clustering.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GUV and DSLB reconstitution experiments shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: A novel cholesterol-binding motif exists in the transmembrane region of human S1R.
source: We identify a novel cholesterol-binding motif in the transmembrane region of human S1R.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and experimental data from mutagenesis and cholesterol-binding assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Mutations of the cholesterol-binding motif impair association of recombinant S1R with cholesterol beads.
source: Mutations of this motif impair association of recombinant S1R with cholesterol beads, affect S1R clustering in vitro and disrupt S1R subcellular localization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cholesterol-agarose pulldown assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations of the cholesterol-binding motif affect S1R clustering in vitro.
source: Mutations of this motif impair association of recombinant S1R with cholesterol beads, affect S1R clustering in vitro and disrupt S1R subcellular localization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GUV reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations of the cholesterol-binding motif disrupt S1R subcellular localization.
source: Mutations of this motif impair association of recombinant S1R with cholesterol beads, affect S1R clustering in vitro and disrupt S1R subcellular localization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cellular imaging experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: S1R-induced membrane microdomains have increased local membrane thickness.
source: We demonstrate that S1R-induced membrane microdomains have increased local membrane thickness and that increased local cholesterol concentration and/or membrane thickness in these microdomains can modulate signaling of inositol-requiring enzyme 1α in the ER.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using MBP-TM molecular rulers shown in Figure 5.

claim: Increased local cholesterol concentration and/or membrane thickness in S1R microdomains can modulate signaling of inositol-requiring enzyme 1α (IRE1α) in the ER.
source: We demonstrate that S1R-induced membrane microdomains have increased local membrane thickness and that increased local cholesterol concentration and/or membrane thickness in these microdomains can modulate signaling of inositol-requiring enzyme 1α in the ER.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from GUV reconstitution and cellular IRE1α signaling assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: S1R agonists cause disruption of S1R clusters.
source: Further, S1R agonists cause disruption of S1R clusters, suggesting that biological activity of S1R agonists is linked to remodeling of ER membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DSLB experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The biological activity of S1R agonists is linked to remodeling of ER membrane microdomains.
source: Further, S1R agonists cause disruption of S1R clusters, suggesting that biological activity of S1R agonists is linked to remodeling of ER membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that agonists disrupt S1R clusters.

claim: The plasma membrane contains 30–40% cholesterol and 10–30% sphingolipids based on molar amounts.
source: The plasma membrane (PM) is highly enriched in cholesterol and other sterols, containing 30–40% cholesterol and 10–30% sphingolipids based on molar amounts (van Meer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Meer et al., 2008.

claim: Cholesterol forms lipid rafts or cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the plasma membrane that play important signaling roles in cells.
source: It is widely accepted that cholesterol is not distributed homogeneously in the PM and instead forms lipid rafts, or cholesterol-enriched microdomains, that play important signaling roles in cells (Levental et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levental et al., 2020 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cholesterol is produced in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Although cholesterol is produced in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the concentration of cholesterol in ER membranes is much lower than in the PM (van Meer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Meer et al., 2008 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The concentration of cholesterol in ER membranes is much lower than in the plasma membrane.
source: Although cholesterol is produced in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the concentration of cholesterol in ER membranes is much lower than in the PM (van Meer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Meer et al., 2008.

claim: The Scap-SREBP pathway maintains ER cholesterol levels with a half-maximal response of SREBP-2 at about 5 molar % cholesterol in the ER.
source: Level of ER cholesterol is maintained by an "on-and-off" switch of the Scap-SREBP pathway with a half-maximal response of SREBP-2 at about 5 molar % cholesterol in the ER (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2008.

claim: Cholesterol-enriched microdomains exist in the ER membrane.
source: There is limited information about spatial distribution of cholesterol in the ER membrane, but recent studies suggested existence of cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER membrane (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; King et al., 2020; Montesinos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; King et al., 2020; Montesinos et al., 2020.

claim: Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs) are sites on the ER membrane in immediate proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: One of the most studied examples of such microdomains are mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), which are sites on the ER membrane in immediate proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane (Csordás et al., 2018; Prinz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Csordás et al., 2018; Prinz et al., 2020.

claim: MAMs play important roles in ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer.
source: MAMs have been shown to play important roles in a variety of cellular functions, such as ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer (Csordás et al., 2018; Hajnóczky et al., 2002), ATP production (Hajnóczky et al., 2002), lipid metabolism (Csordás et al., 2018; Vance, 2014), and autophagy (Garofalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Csordás et al., 2018; Hajnóczky et al., 2002.

claim: MAMs play important roles in ATP production.
source: MAMs have been shown to play important roles in a variety of cellular functions, such as ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer (Csordás et al., 2018; Hajnóczky et al., 2002), ATP production (Hajnóczky et al., 2002), lipid metabolism (Csordás et al., 2018; Vance, 2014), and autophagy (Garofalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hajnóczky et al., 2002.

claim: MAMs play important roles in lipid metabolism.
source: MAMs have been shown to play important roles in a variety of cellular functions, such as ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer (Csordás et al., 2018; Hajnóczky et al., 2002), ATP production (Hajnóczky et al., 2002), lipid metabolism (Csordás et al., 2018; Vance, 2014), and autophagy (Garofalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Csordás et al., 2018; Vance, 2014.

claim: MAMs play important roles in autophagy.
source: MAMs have been shown to play important roles in a variety of cellular functions, such as ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer (Csordás et al., 2018; Hajnóczky et al., 2002), ATP production (Hajnóczky et al., 2002), lipid metabolism (Csordás et al., 2018; Vance, 2014), and autophagy (Garofalo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garofalo et al., 2016.

claim: MAM dysregulation has been observed in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Unsurprisingly, MAM dysregulation was observed in numerous pathophysiological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases (Schon and Area-Gomez, 2013), cancers (Morciano et al., 2018), and lysosomal disorders (Annunziata et al., 2018; Sano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schon and Area-Gomez, 2013.

claim: MAM dysregulation has been observed in cancers.
source: Unsurprisingly, MAM dysregulation was observed in numerous pathophysiological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases (Schon and Area-Gomez, 2013), cancers (Morciano et al., 2018), and lysosomal disorders (Annunziata et al., 2018; Sano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morciano et al., 2018.

claim: MAM dysregulation has been observed in lysosomal disorders.
source: Unsurprisingly, MAM dysregulation was observed in numerous pathophysiological conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases (Schon and Area-Gomez, 2013), cancers (Morciano et al., 2018), and lysosomal disorders (Annunziata et al., 2018; Sano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Annunziata et al., 2018; Sano et al., 2009.

claim: S1R has a short cytoplasmic tail and a large luminal ligand-binding domain.
source: Sigma 1 receptor (S1R) is a 223-amino-acid-long, single-pass transmembrane ER protein (Hayashi, 2019; Ryskamp et al., 2019; Schmidt and Kruse, 2019) that has a short cytoplasmic tail and a large luminal ligand-binding domain (Mavylutov et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mavylutov et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: S1R acts as a molecular chaperone that can stabilize a native conformation of multiple client proteins in stress conditions.
source: It has been suggested that S1R acts as a molecular chaperone that can stabilize a native conformation of multiple client proteins in stress conditions (Hayashi, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2017; Su et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2017; Su et al., 2010.

claim: S1R can act as an RNA-binding protein.
source: Recent studies also suggested that S1R can act as an RNA-binding protein (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: S1R is highly enriched in the liver and expressed in the nervous system.
source: S1R is highly enriched in the liver and expressed in the nervous system.
evidence: This is stated directly and represents established knowledge about S1R expression.

claim: S1R knockout mice reveal nervous system abnormalities.
source: Analysis of S1R knockout (KO) mice revealed a number of nervous system abnormalities (Couly et al., 2020), suggesting that S1R plays an important role in neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Couly et al., 2020.

claim: S1R plays an important role in neurons.
source: Analysis of S1R knockout (KO) mice revealed a number of nervous system abnormalities (Couly et al., 2020), suggesting that S1R plays an important role in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of nervous system abnormalities in S1R KO mice.

claim: Mutations in S1R lead to a juvenile form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in S1R lead to a juvenile form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Al-Saif et al., 2011) and distal hereditary motor neuropathies (dHMNs) (Almendra et al., 2018; Gregianin et al., 2016; Horga et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Ververis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Al-Saif et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations in S1R lead to distal hereditary motor neuropathies (dHMNs) in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in S1R lead to a juvenile form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Al-Saif et al., 2011) and distal hereditary motor neuropathies (dHMNs) (Almendra et al., 2018; Gregianin et al., 2016; Horga et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Ververis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Almendra et al., 2018; Gregianin et al., 2016; Horga et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Ververis et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic ablation of S1R exacerbates pathology of several neurological disorders in animal models.
source: In animal models, genetic ablation of S1R exacerbates pathology of several neurological disorders (Hong et al., 2017a; Mavlyutov et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2017a; Mavlyutov et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2017.

claim: S1R is considered a potential drug target for treatment of neurodegenerative disorders and cancer.
source: S1R is considered to be a potential drug target for treatment of neurodegenerative disorders and cancer (Herrando-Grabulosa et al., 2021; Kim and Maher, 2017; Ryskamp et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herrando-Grabulosa et al., 2021; Kim and Maher, 2017; Ryskamp et al., 2019.

claim: S1R binds multiple classes of drugs with nano- and sub-micromolar affinities.
source: S1R binds multiple classes of drugs with nano- and sub-micromolar affinities (Maurice and Su, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maurice and Su, 2009.

claim: S1R ligands are classified into agonists and antagonists based on their biological activity.
source: Based on their biological activity, S1R ligands are classified into agonists and antagonists (Maurice and Su, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maurice and Su, 2009.

claim: Under resting conditions, S1R forms an inert complex with GRP78/BiP protein in the ER.
source: The most prominent hypothesis is that under resting conditions S1R forms an inert complex with GRP78/BiP protein in the ER (Hayashi and Su, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayashi and Su, 2007.

claim: When activated by agonists or in conditions of cellular stress, S1R dissociates from BiP and is able to interact with a variety of client proteins.
source: When activated by agonists or in conditions of cellular stress, S1R dissociates from BiP and is able to interact with a variety of client proteins (Hayashi and Su, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayashi and Su, 2007.

claim: S1R preferentially localizes to MAMs.
source: S1R preferentially localizes to MAMs (Hayashi and Su, 2007), and genetic KO of S1R in mice results in impaired MAM stability as evidenced by reduced number of contacts on electron micrographs and biochemical fractionation of MAM components (Watanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hayashi and Su, 2007.

claim: Genetic knockout of S1R in mice results in impaired MAM stability as evidenced by reduced number of contacts on electron micrographs and biochemical fractionation of MAM components.
source: S1R preferentially localizes to MAMs (Hayashi and Su, 2007), and genetic KO of S1R in mice results in impaired MAM stability as evidenced by reduced number of contacts on electron micrographs and biochemical fractionation of MAM components (Watanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2016.

claim: MAMs are cholesterol-enriched microdomains within the ER membrane.
source: MAMs are cholesterol-enriched microdomains within the ER membrane (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Montesinos et al., 2020), and previous studies demonstrated that S1R can directly interact with cholesterol and ceramides in MAMs (Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hayashi and Su, 2004; Palmer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Montesinos et al., 2020.

claim: S1R can directly interact with cholesterol and ceramides in MAMs.
source: MAMs are cholesterol-enriched microdomains within the ER membrane (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Montesinos et al., 2020), and previous studies demonstrated that S1R can directly interact with cholesterol and ceramides in MAMs (Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hayashi and Su, 2004; Palmer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hayashi and Su, 2004; Palmer et al., 2007.

claim: S1R-GFP formed puncta in the ER.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Hayashi and Su, 2003a; Hayashi and Su, 2003b), S1R-GFP formed puncta in the ER (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous reports.

claim: S1R-GFP puncta were frequently found in close opposition to mitochondria.
source: To determine if these puncta corresponded to MAMs, we co-stained cells with a mitochondrial marker TOM20 and established that S1R-GFP puncta were frequently found in close opposition to mitochondria (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ALS-causing mutant S1R-E102Q was distributed uniformly in the ER and was not enriched in proximity to mitochondria.
source: In contrast to wild-type (WT) S1R, an ALS-causing mutant S1R-E102Q (Al-Saif et al., 2011) was distributed uniformly in the ER and was not enriched in proximity to mitochondria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Al-Saif et al., 2011.

claim: Protein retention expansion microscopy (pro-ExM) resulted in a 4.0–4.5-fold physical expansion of the specimen.
source: In order to increase the spatial resolution of our experiments, we utilized the protein retention expansion microscopy (pro-ExM) procedure that resulted in a 4.0–4.5-fold physical expansion of the specimen (Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tillberg et al., 2016.

claim: S1R is enriched in areas of mitochondrial proximity along ER tubules.
source: Measurements of signal intensities of mCherry-Sec61b and S1R-GFP markers along the selected ER tubule indicated enrichment of S1R in the areas of mitochondrial proximity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: On average, 12 ± 5% of mCherry-Sec61β signal area overlapped with mitochondria.
source: On average, 12 ± 5% of mCherry-Sec61β signal area overlapped with mitochondria, while a higher degree of overlap was observed for S1R-GFP and mitochondria, with fractional area of 31 ± 7% (n [number of cells] = 5, p-value=0.0034).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: 31 ± 7% of S1R-GFP signal area overlapped with mitochondria.
source: On average, 12 ± 5% of mCherry-Sec61β signal area overlapped with mitochondria, while a higher degree of overlap was observed for S1R-GFP and mitochondria, with fractional area of 31 ± 7% (n [number of cells] = 5, p-value=0.0034).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: Biochemical fractionation of MAMs from mouse liver confirmed enrichment of S1R in MAM fraction.
source: As an alternative approach, we performed a biochemical fractionation of MAMs from mice liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which confirmed enrichment of S1R in MAM fraction.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: S1R-GFP is enriched in ER subdomains in close opposition to mitochondria.
source: Taken together, this data confirmed that S1R-GFP is enriched in ER subdomains in close opposition to mitochondria, consistent with previous reports (Hayashi and Su, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental data and a citation to Hayashi and Su, 2007.

claim: When S1R was reconstituted into liposomes composed of DOPC, it was distributed uniformly.
source: Confocal imaging revealed that when S1R was reconstituted into liposomes composed of 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC), it was distributed uniformly (Figure 2C, left panel) with occasional clustering observed at the sites of contact between different GUVs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When vesicles contained 10% cholesterol, S1R was often clustered.
source: In contrast, when vesicles also contained 10% cholesterol (molar ratio to DOPC), S1R was often clustered (Figure 2C, right panel, marked with asterisks).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: S1R clusters were observed in 7 ± 5% of DOPC liposomes.
source: On average, S1R clusters were observed in 7 ± 5% of DOPC liposomes (n = 3, 506 liposomes) and in 31 ± 3% of DOPC:10 mol % cholesterol liposomes (n = 3, 685 liposomes) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: S1R clusters were observed in 31 ± 3% of DOPC:10 mol % cholesterol liposomes.
source: On average, S1R clusters were observed in 7 ± 5% of DOPC liposomes (n = 3, 506 liposomes) and in 31 ± 3% of DOPC:10 mol % cholesterol liposomes (n = 3, 685 liposomes) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cluster size was higher in the presence of cholesterol (0.16 ± 0.07 μm2 for DOPC GUVs and 0.27 ± 0.19 μm2 for cholesterol-containing liposomes).
source: Cluster size was higher in the presence of cholesterol (0.16 ± 0.07 μm2 for DOPC GUVs and 0.27 ± 0.19 μm2 for cholesterol-containing liposomes) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The average number of clusters per liposome was significantly higher for GUVs containing 10 mol % cholesterol (λ = 0.15 for DOPC GUVs and λ = 0.72 for cholesterol-containing liposomes, p<0.001).
source: We determined that the average number of clusters per liposome was significantly higher for GUVs containing 10 mol % cholesterol (λ = 0.15 for DOPC GUVs and λ = 0.72 for cholesterol-containing liposomes, p<0.001, N1 = 194, N2 = 201) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Presence of cholesterol can promote clustering of S1R in lipid membranes.
source: From these results, we concluded that presence of cholesterol can promote clustering of S1R in the lipid membranes and proposed that association with cholesterol plays a direct role in S1R-induced formation of ER membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased S1R clustering in the presence of cholesterol.

claim: Association with cholesterol plays a direct role in S1R-induced formation of ER membrane microdomains.
source: From these results, we concluded that presence of cholesterol can promote clustering of S1R in the lipid membranes and proposed that association with cholesterol plays a direct role in S1R-induced formation of ER membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental data showing cholesterol-dependent S1R clustering.

claim: Previous studies identified Y173 and Y201/Y206 as potential sites of S1R association with cholesterol.
source: S1R was shown to interact with cholesterol, other sterols, and sphingolipids in binding studies (Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hulce et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2007). Previous studies identified two potential sites of S1R association with cholesterol – Y173 and Y201/Y206 (Palmer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Palmer et al., 2007.

claim: In the S1R crystal structure, Y173 localizes adjacent to the S1R ligand-binding domain and has no membrane contact.
source: However, in the S1R crystal structure (Schmidt et al., 2016) Y173 localizes adjacent to the S1R ligand-binding domain and has no membrane contact, and Y201 and Y206 are located within the C-terminal membrane-adjacent amphipathic helices.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the S1R crystal structure from Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: Y201 and Y206 are located within the C-terminal membrane-adjacent amphipathic helices.
source: However, in the S1R crystal structure (Schmidt et al., 2016) Y173 localizes adjacent to the S1R ligand-binding domain and has no membrane contact, and Y201 and Y206 are located within the C-terminal membrane-adjacent amphipathic helices.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the S1R crystal structure from Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: Tandem CARC-like motifs exist in the transmembrane helix of S1R spanning amino acids R7-L14.
source: Additional sequence analysis revealed tandem CARC-like (reverse sequence for the cholesterol-recognition amino acid consensus) motifs R/K-X1-5-Y/F/W-X1-5-L/V (PLEASE KEEP AMINO ACID SEQUENCE ON 1 LINE) (Fantini and Barrantes, 2013) in the transmembrane helix of S1R that span amino acids R7-L14 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation to Fantini and Barrantes, 2013.

claim: Wild-type S1R and the S1R-Y201S/Y206S mutant each formed puncta in the ER.
source: Wild-type S1R and the S1R-Y201S/Y206S mutant each formed puncta in the ER (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The S1R distribution in the ER was diffuse for the S1R-Y173S, S1R-4G, and S1R-W9L/W11L mutants.
source: In contrast, the S1R distribution in the ER was diffuse for the S1R-Y173S, S1R-4G, and S1R-W9L/W11L mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The puncta observed with wild-type S1R and Y201S/Y206S mutant corresponded to MAMs.
source: By performing TOM20-staining experiments, we confirmed that the puncta observed with the wild-type S1R and Y201S/Y206S mutant corresponded to MAMs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For wild-type S1R, Mander's coefficient was M = 0.50 ± 0.02.
source: For wild-type S1R, Mander's coefficient was M = 0.50 ± 0.02 (n = 3, 25 cells), indicating that not all mCherry-Sec61β signal colocalized with the GFP signal in S1R clusters (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.77 ± 0.09 for S1R-Y173S.
source: In contrast, Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.77 ± 0.09 (n = 2, 11 cells) for S1R-Y173S, 0.72 ± 0.04 (n = 3, 30 cells) for S1R-4G, and 0.77 ± 0.03 (n = 3, 17 cells) for S1R-W9L/W11L (Figure 3C), reflecting more diffuse distribution patterns.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.72 ± 0.04 for S1R-4G.
source: In contrast, Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.77 ± 0.09 (n = 2, 11 cells) for S1R-Y173S, 0.72 ± 0.04 (n = 3, 30 cells) for S1R-4G, and 0.77 ± 0.03 (n = 3, 17 cells) for S1R-W9L/W11L (Figure 3C), reflecting more diffuse distribution patterns.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.77 ± 0.03 for S1R-W9L/W11L.
source: In contrast, Mander's coefficient was equal to 0.77 ± 0.09 (n = 2, 11 cells) for S1R-Y173S, 0.72 ± 0.04 (n = 3, 30 cells) for S1R-4G, and 0.77 ± 0.03 (n = 3, 17 cells) for S1R-W9L/W11L (Figure 3C), reflecting more diffuse distribution patterns.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mander's coefficient for the S1R-Y201S/Y206S mutant was equal to 0.49 ± 0.16, similar to the wild type.
source: Mander's coefficient for the S1R-Y201S/Y206S mutant was equal to 0.49 ± 0.16 (n = 2, 12 cells) (Figure 3C), similar to the wild type.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The newly identified CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to MAMs.
source: Taken together, we concluded that the newly identified CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to MAMs and that the Y201/Y206 motif is dispensable.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that mutations in the CARC motif disrupt MAM localization.

claim: The Y201/Y206 motif is dispensable for S1R targeting to MAMs.
source: Taken together, we concluded that the newly identified CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to MAMs and that the Y201/Y206 motif is dispensable.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the Y201S/Y206S mutant behaves similarly to wild-type S1R.

claim: S1R-GFP appeared enriched in ER-PM junctions marked by MAPPER.
source: As reported previously, MAPPER (shown in red) formed small punctate patterns corresponding to the ER membrane in close proximity to the PM (Figure 3D). S1R-GFP appeared enriched in these same puncta (Figure 3D), in agreement with the previous report (Srivats et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Srivats et al., 2016.

claim: S1R-4G and S1R-W9L/W11L were distributed diffusely in the ER.
source: S1R-4G and S1R-W9L/W11L were distributed diffusely in the ER (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For wild-type S1R-GFP, 16 ± 7% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions.
source: For wild-type S1R-GFP, 16 ± 7% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions compared to 7 ± 5% for S1R-4G mutant and 5 ± 3% for S1R-W9L/W11L mutant (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: For S1R-4G mutant, 7 ± 5% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions.
source: For wild-type S1R-GFP, 16 ± 7% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions compared to 7 ± 5% for S1R-4G mutant and 5 ± 3% for S1R-W9L/W11L mutant (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: For S1R-W9L/W11L mutant, 5 ± 3% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions.
source: For wild-type S1R-GFP, 16 ± 7% of the fluorescence signal was localized to the ER-PM junctions compared to 7 ± 5% for S1R-4G mutant and 5 ± 3% for S1R-W9L/W11L mutant (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Wild-type S1R localizes to and is enriched in ER contact sites such as MAMs and ER-PM junctions.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that wild-type S1R localizes to and is enriched in ER contact sites such as MAMs and ER-PM junctions and that CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to these sites.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of experimental data showing S1R enrichment at these sites.

claim: CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to ER contact sites.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that wild-type S1R localizes to and is enriched in ER contact sites such as MAMs and ER-PM junctions and that CARC motif is important for S1R targeting to these sites.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations in the CARC motif disrupt S1R localization to these sites.

claim: The S1R-W9L/W11L mutant formed less clusters in GUVs with 10 mol % cholesterol.
source: The S1R-W9L/W11L mutant formed less clusters (Figure 4A, B), consistent with the diffuse distribution of this mutant in cells (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: S1R-4G still formed clusters when reconstituted in GUVs with 10 mol % cholesterol, similar to the wild-type S1R.
source: However, S1R-4G still formed clusters when reconstituted in GUVs, similar to the wild-type S1R (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: The W9L/W11L mutation abolished S1R association with cholesterol.
source: To explain these results, we reasoned that the W9L/W11L mutation abolished S1R association with cholesterol, but the 4G mutation only weakened it as this mutation still contains the CARC consensus sequence (Fantini and Barrantes, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and knowledge about CARC motifs.

claim: The 4G mutation only weakened S1R association with cholesterol.
source: To explain these results, we reasoned that the W9L/W11L mutation abolished S1R association with cholesterol, but the 4G mutation only weakened it as this mutation still contains the CARC consensus sequence (Fantini and Barrantes, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and knowledge about CARC motifs.

claim: Recombinant S1R binds to cholesterol agarose.
source: First, we confirmed that recombinant S1R binds to cholesterol agarose, but not to the control resin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both S1R-4G and S1R-W9L/W11L mutants have reduced affinity for cholesterol in pulldown assays with purified recombinant protein.
source: We then tested S1R-4G and S1R-W9L/W11L mutants. Based on obtained results, we concluded that both mutants have reduced affinity for cholesterol (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: S1R-W9L/W11L-6His bound to cholesterol agarose significantly weaker than the wild-type S1R in pulldown assays from cell lysates.
source: We found that S1R-W9L/W11L-6His bound to cholesterol agarose significantly weaker than the wild-type S1R (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: S1R-4G-6His behaved similar to the wild-type S1R-6His in pulldown assays from cell lysates.
source: In contrast, S1R-4G-6His behaved similar to the wild-type S1R-6His in these experiments (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: W9L/W11L mutation disrupted cholesterol binding to a much greater extent than 4G mutation.
source: Taken together, we concluded that W9L/W11L mutation disrupted cholesterol binding to a much greater extent than 4G mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of pulldown assay results for both mutants.

claim: 4G mutation leads to diffuse distribution of S1R in cells because ER cholesterol levels in cells are no more than 5 mol %.
source: We reason that 4G mutation leads to diffuse distribution of S1R in cells (Figure 3B) because ER cholesterol levels in cells are no more than 5 mol % (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and knowledge about ER cholesterol levels.

claim: ER cholesterol levels are sufficient for association with wild-type S1R but not with S1R-4G mutant that has reduced affinity for cholesterol.
source: Presumably, these levels of cholesterol are sufficient for association with wild-type S1R but not with S1R-4G mutant that has reduced affinity for cholesterol.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: The length of the S1R transmembrane domain is 24 amino acids.
source: Interestingly, according to the crystal structure and hydrophobicity analysis, the length of the S1R transmembrane (TM) domain is 24 a.a (Figure 3A; Schmidt et al., 2016), which is longer than a typical 20 a.a TM length of ER-resident proteins (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure and supported by citations.

claim: The S1R transmembrane domain is longer than a typical 20 amino acid TM length of ER-resident proteins.
source: Interestingly, according to the crystal structure and hydrophobicity analysis, the length of the S1R transmembrane (TM) domain is 24 a.a (Figure 3A; Schmidt et al., 2016), which is longer than a typical 20 a.a TM length of ER-resident proteins (Sharpe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with established knowledge about ER protein TM lengths.

claim: The length of the S1R TM domain is estimated to be 36.9 Å.
source: The length of the S1R TM domain is estimated to be 36.9 Å and should have a positive hydrophobic mismatch when compared to a DOPC bilayer, which has a hydrophobic thickness of 26.8 Å (Kučerka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is calculated based on structural data and supported by a citation.

claim: A DOPC bilayer has a hydrophobic thickness of 26.8 Å.
source: The length of the S1R TM domain is estimated to be 36.9 Å and should have a positive hydrophobic mismatch when compared to a DOPC bilayer, which has a hydrophobic thickness of 26.8 Å (Kučerka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kučerka et al., 2006.

claim: A cholesterol-rich DOPC bilayer has a hydrophobic thickness of 36.0 Å, matching well with the S1R TM length.
source: In contrast, a cholesterol-rich DOPC bilayer has a hydrophobic thickness of 36.0 Å, matching well with the S1R TM length (Milovanovic and Jahn, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Milovanovic and Jahn, 2015.

claim: S1R clustering in ER membrane is influenced by local changes in membrane thickness.
source: It is therefore possible that S1R clustering in ER membrane is influenced by local changes in membrane thickness, as has been described for the targeting of plasma membrane proteins to lipid rafts (Lorent et al., 2017).
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural analysis and supported by a citation to Lorent et al., 2017.

claim: The S1R-Δ4 mutant displayed a more diffuse distribution in the ER when compared to the wild-type S1R.
source: When S1R-Δ4 GFP-fusion protein was expressed in HEK293 cells, it displayed a more diffuse distribution in the ER when compared to the wild-type S1R (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mander's coefficient for S1R-Δ4 mutant is 0.72 ± 0.07 compared to 0.50 ± 0.02 for the wild-type protein.
source: Mander's coefficient for this mutant is 0.72 ± 0.07 (n = 3, 27 cells) compared to Mander's coefficient of 0.50 ± 0.02 for the wild-type protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: S1R did not form clusters in DNPC GUVs neither in the absence nor in the presence of 20% cholesterol.
source: S1R did not form clusters in DNPC GUVs neither in the absence nor in the presence of 20% cholesterol (0%: 6.8%, 92 liposomes, 20%: 2.9%, 77 liposomes) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Local increase in membrane thickness contributes to S1R targeting to cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER.
source: From these results, we concluded that local increase in membrane thickness contributes to S1R targeting to cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that S1R does not cluster in thick DNPC bilayers.

claim: By clustering with cholesterol, S1R can promote the formation of microdomains with thicker bilayer structure.
source: We then hypothesized that by clustering with cholesterol, S1R can also promote the formation of microdomains with thicker bilayer structure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: In cholesterol-free conditions, MBP-TM17 was distributed largely uniformly in the GUV membrane while MBP-TM27 was enriched at the junctions between the individual GUVs.
source: We found that in the cholesterol-free conditions , MBP-TM17 was distributed largely uniformly in the GUV membrane while MBP-TM27 was enriched at the junctions between the individual GUVs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cholesterol had little effect on the distribution of MBP-TMs.
source: Cholesterol had little effect on the distribution of MBP-TMs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MBP-TM27 localized to the GUV junction sites based on a hydrophobic matching mechanism.
source: We hypothesized that MBP-TM27 localized to the GUV junction sites based on a hydrophobic matching mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: When MBP-TM proteins were co-reconstituted with S1R in the presence of 20% cholesterol, MBP-TM17 remained largely diffuse while MBP-TM27 formed clusters that colocalized with S1R clusters.
source: When these rulers were reconstituted together with S1R in the presence of 20% cholesterol, they displayed a different behavior: while MBP-TM17 remained largely diffuse (Figure 5E, top panel), MBP-TM27 formed clusters that colocalized with S1R clusters (Figure 5E, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MBP-TM27 was enriched in S1R domains, while MBP-TM17 showed no partitioning to S1R clusters.
source: Analysis of linear density of MBP-TM proteins inside and outside S1R clusters confirmed that MBP-TM27 was enriched in S1R domains, while MBP-TM17 showed no partitioning to S1R clusters (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Recruitment and clustering events were mainly driven by lipid-protein interactions.
source: Importantly, this behavior was observed for an artificially designed MBP-TM27 protein, suggesting that recruitment and clustering events were mainly driven by lipid-protein interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that an artificial protein shows similar behavior.

claim: In the presence of cholesterol, S1R induces formation of membrane microdomains with increased local thickness.
source: These results suggested that in the presence of cholesterol S1R induces formation of membrane microdomains with increased local thickness.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing enrichment of MBP-TM27 in S1R clusters.

claim: S1R and IRE1α localize in close proximity to each other in the ER.
source: S1R and IRE1α localize in a close proximity to each other in the ER, but do not necessarily interact directly (Rosen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rosen et al., 2019.

claim: IRE1α oligomerization and stress-response activity can be modulated by the surrounding lipid environment.
source: In addition to protein-protein interactions, IRE1α oligomerization and stress-response activity can be also modulated by the surrounding lipid environment (Cho et al., 2019; Halbleib et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2019; Halbleib et al., 2017.

claim: Loading ER with cholesterol affects IRE1α signaling.
source: Loading ER with cholesterol affects IRE1α signaling (Feng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feng et al., 2003.

claim: Significantly more biotinylated IRE1α was pulled down from cells expressing S1R-APEX2 than from cells expressing APEX2-KDEL or Sec61β-APEX2 control constructs.
source: Significantly more biotinylated IRE1α was pulled down from the cells expressed S1R-APEX2 than from the cells expressing APEX2-KDEL or Sec61β-APEX2 control constructs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The results suggest close proximity of IRE1α and S1R-APEX2.
source: These results suggested close proximity of IRE1α and S1R-APEX2, consistent with the previous studies (Mori et al., 2013; Rosen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the APEX2 proximity labeling data and supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of cholesterol, the distributions of MBP-IRE1α-TM and S1R were uniform.
source: In the absence of cholesterol, the distributions of MBP-IRE1α-TM and S1R were uniform (Figure 5G, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the presence of 20% cholesterol, MBP-IRE1α-TM was recruited to S1R-positive clusters.
source: However, in the presence of 20% cholesterol, MBP-IRE1α-TM was recruited to S1R-positive clusters (Figure 5G, H, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5G, H.

claim: The transmembrane domain of IRE1α partitions into a lipid microenvironment established by S1R in the presence of cholesterol.
source: These results suggested that the transmembrane domain of IRE1α partitions into a lipid microenvironment established by S1R in the presence of cholesterol.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing recruitment of MBP-IRE1α-TM to S1R clusters.

claim: Under resting conditions, the level of phosphorylated IRE1α was lower in S1R KO cells when compared to wild-type cells.
source: We determined that under resting conditions the level of phosphorylated IRE1α was lower in S1R KO cells when compared to wild-type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under ER stress conditions, the same peak level of IRE1α phosphorylation could not be achieved in S1R KO cells.
source: Under ER stress conditions, the same peak level of IRE1α phosphorylation could not be achieved in S1R KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and total cellular response, measured as integrated area under the curve (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), was significantly smaller in S1R KO cells compared to WT, suggesting an impairement in IRE1α signaling.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Total cellular IRE1α response was significantly smaller in S1R KO cells compared to WT, suggesting an impairment in IRE1α signaling.
source: Under ER stress conditions, the same peak level of IRE1α phosphorylation could not be achieved in S1R KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and total cellular response, measured as integrated area under the curve (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), was significantly smaller in S1R KO cells compared to WT, suggesting an impairement in IRE1α signaling.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Production of XBP1s was delayed in S1R KO cells when compared to wild-type cells.
source: We found that production of XBP1s was delayed in S1R KO cells when compared to wild-type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recruitment of IRE1α to S1R-organized microdomains in the ER facilitated IRE1α-mediated signaling.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that recruitment of IRE1α to S1R-organized microdomains in the ER facilitated IRE1α-mediated signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing impaired IRE1α signaling in S1R KO cells.

claim: The conclusions are supported by previously reported inhibition of IRE1α activity in cells transfected with S1R RNAi.
source: Our conclusions are supported by previously reported inhibition of IRE1α activity in cells transfected with S1R RNAi (Mori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mori et al., 2013.

claim: S1Rs can redistribute in the ER upon ligand stimulation.
source: Previous research indicated that S1Rs can redistribute in the ER upon ligand stimulation (Hayashi and Su, 2003a; Hayashi and Su, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi and Su, 2003a; Hayashi and Su, 2007.

claim: The threshold for S1R clustering was in a narrow range between 2.5 and 5.0 mol % cholesterol.
source: The threshold for S1R clustering was in a narrow range between 2.5 and 5.0 mol % (Figure 6C, black line), consistent with a typical ER cholesterol content (Radhakrishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and a citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2008.

claim: Small S1R clusters most likely corresponded to S1R trimers, containing on average 2.65 ± 0.58 molecules.
source: This analysis revealed that small S1R clusters most likely corresponded to S1R trimers, containing on average 2.65 ± 0.58 (n = 47) molecules, consistent with the crystal structure of the protein (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and a citation to Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: The number of S1R molecules in large clusters was widely distributed in a range between tens and hundreds of molecules, with a mean value of 38 molecules per cluster at 20 mol % cholesterol.
source: The number of S1R molecules in the large clusters was widely distributed in a range between tens and hundreds of molecules, with a mean value of 38 molecules per cluster at 20 mol % cholesterol (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Following photobleaching, the recovery of NBD-PC signal was complete outside of S1R clusters (Ymax(out)=1.01 ± 0.06) but incomplete inside these clusters (Ymax(in)=0.74 ± 0.07, p=0.008).
source: Following photobleaching, the recovery of NBD-PC signal was complete outside of S1R clusters (Ymax(out)=1.01 ± 0.06) but incomplete inside these clusters (Ymax(in)=0.74 ± 0.07, p=0.008) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Higher immobile fraction indicates that a fraction of molecules was immobilized at the bleached spot due to being trapped in rigid domains.
source: Higher immobile fraction indicates that a fraction of molecules was immobilized at the bleached spot due to the fact that they were trapped in rigid domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data.

claim: Lateral mobility of the lipids within S1R clusters is reduced, consistent with known properties of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane.
source: These data suggest that lateral mobility of the lipids within S1R clusters is reduced, consistent with known properties of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane (Sezgin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data and supported by a citation to Sezgin et al., 2017.

claim: Addition of selective S1R agonist (+)-SKF-10047 at the time of the second bilayer formation reduced the number of large S1R clusters.
source: Addition of selective S1R agonist (+)-SKF-10047 at the time of the second bilayer formation reduced the number of large S1R clusters (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effects of (+)-SKF-10047 on S1R clustering were concentration-dependent, with half-maximal effect observed at 50 nM.
source: The effects of (+)-SKF-10047 on S1R clustering were concentration-dependent, with half-maximal effect observed at 50 nM (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effects of (+)-SKF-10047 were blocked by the addition of a S1R antagonist NE-100.
source: The effects of (+)-SKF-10047 were blocked by the addition of a S1R antagonist NE-100 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Agonists resulted in reduced cluster size.
source: Consistently, agonists resulted in reduced cluster size (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: S1R agonists prevented formation of S1R clusters or promoted disassembly of S1R clusters in the membrane.
source: These results suggested that S1R agonists prevented formation of S1R clusters or promoted disassembly of S1R clusters in the membrane and that these effects could be blocked by S1R antagonists.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced clustering in the presence of agonists.

claim: The effects of S1R agonists on clustering could be blocked by S1R antagonists.
source: These results suggested that S1R agonists prevented formation of S1R clusters or promoted disassembly of S1R clusters in the membrane and that these effects could be blocked by S1R antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that NE-100 blocks the effects of (+)-SKF-10047.

claim: The results are consistent with previous biochemical studies that demonstrated that the proportion of S1R multimers formed in cells was decreased by the agonists (+)-pentazocine and PRE-084 but increased by the antagonists CM304, haloperidol, and NE-100.
source: Our results are consistent with previous biochemical studies that demonstrated that the proportion of S1R multimers formed in cells was decreased by the agonists (+)-pentazocine and PRE-084 but increased by the antagonists CM304, haloperidol, and NE-100 (Hong, 2020; Hong et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hong, 2020; Hong et al., 2017b.

claim: The results are consistent with effects of (+)-pentazocine and haloperidol described in FRET experiments performed with cells transfected with fluorescently tagged S1Rs.
source: These results are also consistent with effects of (+)-pentazocine and haloperidol described in FRET experiments performed with cells transfected with fluorescently tagged S1Rs (Mishra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mishra et al., 2015.

claim: It has been reported that S1R agonists such as (+)-pentazocine and PRE-084 stabilized the oligomeric state of purified S1R in the presence of detergents.
source: In contrast, it has been reported that S1R agonists such as (+)-pentazocine and PRE-084 stabilized the oligomeric state of purified S1R in the presence of detergents (Gromek et al., 2014), suggesting that biochemical properties of S1R in the membrane and in detergent may differ from each other.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gromek et al., 2014.

claim: Biochemical properties of S1R in the membrane and in detergent may differ from each other.
source: In contrast, it has been reported that S1R agonists such as (+)-pentazocine and PRE-084 stabilized the oligomeric state of purified S1R in the presence of detergents (Gromek et al., 2014), suggesting that biochemical properties of S1R in the membrane and in detergent may differ from each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between results in membranes and detergents.

claim: S1R participates in the formation of thicker cholesterol-rich lipid clusters.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that S1R participates in the formation of thicker cholesterol-rich lipid clusters and S1R agonists act by disassembling these membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing S1R clustering in cholesterol-rich membranes.

claim: S1R agonists act by disassembling cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that S1R participates in the formation of thicker cholesterol-rich lipid clusters and S1R agonists act by disassembling these membrane microdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that agonists reduce S1R clustering.

claim: The biological activity of S1R in cells can be explained by the ability of this protein to form cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER.
source: Based on our results, we propose that the biological activity of S1R in cells can be explained by the ability of this protein to form cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER, therefore acting as ER lipid scaffolding protein.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: S1R acts as an ER lipid scaffolding protein.
source: Based on our results, we propose that the biological activity of S1R in cells can be explained by the ability of this protein to form cholesterol-enriched microdomains in the ER, therefore acting as ER lipid scaffolding protein.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: A role of S1R in organization and remodeling of lipid raft microdomains in the plasma membrane has been proposed previously based on cell biological studies.
source: A role of S1R in organization and remodeling of lipid raft microdomains in the plasma membrane has been proposed previously based on cell biological studies (Palmer et al., 2007; Vollrath et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palmer et al., 2007; Vollrath et al., 2014.

claim: S1R microdomains have increased local membrane thickness, providing a favorable environment for recruitment of ER proteins with longer transmembrane domains.
source: Our data further suggest that such microdomains have increased local membrane thickness, providing a favorable environment for recruitment of ER proteins with longer transmembrane domains (Lorent et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation to Lorent et al., 2017.

claim: Increased local cholesterol concentration and membrane thickness can modulate activity of ER proteins recruited to S1R microdomains.
source: Increased local cholesterol concentration and membrane thickness can modulate activity of ER proteins recruited to these microdomains.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effects on IRE1α signaling.

claim: The hypothesis may explain how a small protein such as S1R is able to modulate activity of almost a hundred effector proteins.
source: Our hypothesis may explain how a small protein such as S1R is able to modulate activity of almost a hundred effector proteins (Couly et al., 2020; Delprat et al., 2020; Kourrich et al., 2012; Ryskamp et al., 2019; Schmidt and Kruse, 2019).
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: Activity of S1R effector proteins could be affected by changes in local lipid microenvironment and not only via protein-protein interactions with the S1R.
source: We reason that activity of these proteins could be affected by changes in local lipid microenvironment and not only via protein-protein interactions with the S1R.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Micrometer-sized large intracellular vesicles exhibit phase-separation behavior at contact sites between the ER and mitochondria, plasma membrane and lipid droplets.
source: A recent study demonstrated that micrometer-sized large intracellular vesicles exhibit phase-separation behavior at contact sites between the ER and mitochondria, plasma membrane and lipid droplets (King et al., 2020), similar to phase separation observed in giant plasma membrane-derived vesicles (Levental et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to King et al., 2020 and Levental et al., 2011.

claim: MAMs are enriched in cholesterol and ceramides.
source: It has been shown that MAMs are enriched in cholesterol and ceramides (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hayashi and Su, 2003a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Hayashi and Su, 2003a.

claim: S1R can contribute to stabilization and/or formation of cholesterol-rich lipid microdomains in the ER membrane.
source: Our findings suggest that S1R can contribute to stabilization and/or formation of these cholesterol-rich lipid microdomains in the ER membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: This conclusion is consistent with MAM defects observed in S1R KO mice.
source: This conclusion is consistent with MAM defects observed in S1R KO mice (Watanabe et al., 2016), with earlier analysis of S1R targeting to detergent-resistant domains in the ER (Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010), and with previous suggestions that S1R contributes to stability of lipid rafts in the plasma membrane (Palmer et al., 2007; Vollrath et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Watanabe et al., 2016; Hayashi and Fujimoto, 2010; Palmer et al., 2007; Vollrath et al., 2014.

claim: Activities of several ER channels including ryanodine receptors, sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase, and inositol-1,4,5-triphosphate receptors can be modulated by cholesterol content, lipid packing, or membrane thickness.
source: It was shown in direct and indirect experiments that activities of several ER channels including ryanodine receptors, sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase, and inositol-1,4,5-triphosphate receptors can be modulated by cholesterol content, lipid packing, or membrane thickness (Cannon et al., 2003; Gustavsson et al., 2011; Li et al., 2004; Madden et al., 1979; Sano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cannon et al., 2003; Gustavsson et al., 2011; Li et al., 2004; Madden et al., 1979; Sano et al., 2009.

claim: Components of the gamma secretase complex reside at MAMs.
source: Components of the gamma secretase complex reside at MAMs, and the transmembrane region of amyloid precursor protein (APP) contains cholesterol-binding motifs (Montesinos et al., 2020; Pera et al., 2017), suggesting modulatory effects of cholesterol on APP processing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montesinos et al., 2020; Pera et al., 2017.

claim: The transmembrane region of amyloid precursor protein (APP) contains cholesterol-binding motifs.
source: Components of the gamma secretase complex reside at MAMs, and the transmembrane region of amyloid precursor protein (APP) contains cholesterol-binding motifs (Montesinos et al., 2020; Pera et al., 2017), suggesting modulatory effects of cholesterol on APP processing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montesinos et al., 2020; Pera et al., 2017.

claim: Several ER stress sensors, including IRE1α, can sense membrane saturation and be activated without protein unfolding in the ER lumen.
source: Several ER stress sensors, including IRE1α, can sense membrane saturation and be activated without protein unfolding in the ER lumen (Ballweg et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2019; Halbleib et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ballweg et al., 2020; Cho et al., 2019; Halbleib et al., 2017.

claim: S1R can exist in an oligomeric form.
source: S1R can exist in an oligomeric form (Gromek et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gromek et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2015.

claim: A photoaffinity probe labeled high-molecular weight oligomers in rat liver microsomes.
source: Originally, a photoaffinity probe labeled high-molecular weight oligomers in rat liver microsomes (Pal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pal et al., 2007.

claim: High-molecular weight species up to 400 kDa were detected in membrane preparations using various biochemical approaches.
source: High-molecular weight species up to 400 kDa were later detected in membrane preparations using various biochemical approaches (Yano et al., 2018; Yano et al., 2019), and a similar wide molecular weight distribution was observed for the recombinant protein (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yano et al., 2018; Yano et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: S1R oligomers form continuous molecular weight distribution ranging from trimers to large (10–100 subunits) clusters.
source: In our experiments, we observed that S1R oligomers form continuous molecular weight distribution ranging from trimers to large (10–100 subunits) clusters (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Formation of large S1R clusters was facilitated by the presence of cholesterol.
source: Formation of large clusters was facilitated by the presence of cholesterol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from DSLB experiments.

claim: The results are consistent with ligand effects observed by native electrophoresis from cell membranes and S1R-BiP association.
source: Our results are consistent with ligand effects observed by native electrophoresis from cell membranes and S1R-BiP association (Hayashi and Su, 2007; Hong, 2020; Hong et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi and Su, 2007; Hong, 2020; Hong et al., 2017b.

claim: Many biological functions of S1R can be explained by its ability to organize and remodel cholesterol-enriched ER microdomains, which in turn affects activity of ER signaling proteins, stress-response, and metabolic status of the cells.
source: In conclusion, we propose that many biological functions of S1R can be explained by its ability to organize and remodel cholesterol-enriched ER microdomains, which in turn affects activity of ER signaling proteins, stress-response, and metabolic status of the cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed based on all the experimental findings.
